extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history; scholars interested in Homeric-era Greek art
extracted.subtask_description: Close-critical analysis of early (heroic-age) Greek art as represented in Homer and archaeological finds, focusing on materials, techniques, composition, and foreign influences. Useful for evaluating authenticity, origin, and aesthetic character of early Greek metal-work, architecture, and mythic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor arts as complementary background
rubrics_metrics.description: Need that world of the minor arts as a complementary background for the higher and more austere Greek sculpture; Greek art begins in a period of refined and exquisite tectonics (crafts subordinate to architecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing sculpture or monumental works, consider small-scale 'tectonic' crafts (metal-work, inlay, carved ornament) as contextual background that shapes style and taste; early development is interdependent with these minor arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homer as evidence for heroic-age art
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer may be regarded as an authority for the character and outward local colouring of the heroic age; the Iliad and Odyssey are earliest pictures of that heroic life and its art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Homeric passages (e.g., shield of Achilles, house of Alcinous) as primary literary evidence to infer the appearance, material use, and social role of early Greek objects—while allowing for poetic enlargement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish use of precious materials and skilful handiwork
rubrics_metrics.description: A delight in the application of precious material and skilful handiwork to personal and domestic adornment — especially graceful metal-work — characterises the heroic-age aesthetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artifacts for the extent and refinement of precious-material use (gold, silver, ivory, amber) and fine metal-working techniques as markers of aesthetic sensibility and social function (ornament, status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal evidence of reality in poetic description
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute, delighted, loving descriptions of details of ornament in Homer are the warrant of a certain amount of truth in what he describes; such internal evidence signals acquaintance with real works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat detailed, technically plausible literary descriptions as possible testimony to real objects; distinguish genuine internal realism from mere fanciful poetical ornament when reconstructing early art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness of early metal-work (touch of the workman's hand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early hammer-work, with pins or riveting rather than soldering, leaves traces of the shaping instruments and the highly trained hand—this tactile expressiveness is a special charm of early metal-work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metal artifacts for evidence of hand-hammering, tool marks, riveting, embossing (empaestik) and similar techniques; such technical signatures indicate authenticity, artisan skill, and aesthetic value tied to manual contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and beauty undivided (functional aesthetics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and beauty are still undivided; objects made for practical ends (cups, cauldrons, chariots, toilet implements) retain fascination and aesthetic value equally for workmen and spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate objects both for their functional design and their decorative treatment; an object's beauty is not separate from its utility in the heroic-age context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and heraldic order in reliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositional method corresponds to practical armourer's or craftsman's arrangement: concentric plates, superimposed rings, and 'heraldic' spacing out of subjects (e.g., city at peace vs city besieged, seasonal balances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting reliefs and painted compositions, attend to concentric structuring, balancing of themes, and the sequence of depiction (centre boss to outer rim)—these formal devices reflect contemporary compositional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic or miraculous attributes as testimony to excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of miraculous or animate properties in objects (golden images that move, armour that lifts like wings) often derive from strong impressions of real, excellent workmanship and therefore can be read as indirect testimony to high quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss mythic exaggeration outright; where miraculous attributions are grounded in vivid descriptive detail, they may indicate that objects originally inspired powerful aesthetic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware conflating antiquity/curiosity with beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic critic must guard against confusing mere curiosity or antiquity with beauty; excavated 'curiosities' may be interesting historically but not necessarily beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply aesthetic criteria (design, proportion, economy of purpose) rather than novelty or rarity alone when judging the beauty of archaeological finds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical indicators of manufacture and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: Details of manufacture—thin metal plates beaten over wooden models, fastening with nails or rivets (no soldering), embossing called empaestik—are concrete evidence of technique and period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed manufacturing techniques (construction methods, fastening, surface treatment) to infer chronological placement, workshop practices, and cultural connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tectonic ornament versus architectural substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Greek building ornament often appears as 'tectonic' (ornament borrowed from crafts like metal-work and inlay) rather than strictly architectural decoration; interiors were frequently lined with metal reliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate ornament derived from minor crafts (tectonic) from structural architectural innovation when assessing early buildings; consider how non-architectural crafts informed architectural appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracing foreign influences and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin and development of Greek art show connections ultimately with Assyria and proximately with Phoenicia and Cyprus (material sources such as ivory, amber, and metals mediated through Phoenician trade), rather than primarily from Egypt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stylistic and material affinities (trade goods, island intermediaries like Cyprus, and parallels in figure types) to trace external influences; consider maritime geography and commerce as vectors of artistic transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth and material culture as mutual reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology (e.g., Pygmalion, cults like that of Hera) reflects the ways of life and thought of the people and thus provides evidence about art's social role and values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mythological motifs and cultic practice to inform interpretations of objects' meanings, functions, and cultural importance, recognizing that myth and material culture are mutually informative.
